title: pytrends Is Dead: A Working Google Trends API Alternative
summary: pytrends broke for good in 2025. See why it fails, what trendspy and the official alpha API offer, and how Wire replaces it…
body_markdown:
If you just ran the first example from pytrends' own README and got a 429 Too Many Requests error, you haven't been rate-limited. You've hit a library whose last release shipped in April 2023 and whose repository was archived in April 2025, and you're now looking for a Google Trends API alternative that works.


[pytrends](https://github.com/GeneralMills/pytrends) was archived by its maintainer on April 17, 2025. The repository is read-only now: a banner says so at the top of the page, and the README still says "Looking for maintainers!" The library wraps Google Trends' internal, undocumented API, and when Google changed its consent flow, nobody was left to patch it. The error isn't Google blocking you for scraping too much. It's pytrends never acquiring the NID cookie that the current flow expects, so Google rejects the request as sent.[Scrapfly's own test on Sep 11, 2026](https://scrapfly.io/blog/posts/google-trends-api-alternatives) found the interest_over_time, interest_by_region and related_queries calls still working that day, but all three of the trending-search methods returning a flat 404, because Google moved that endpoint entirely. Results vary by the week you test. That's the real problem: a library with no maintainer can't tell you which parts still work.


This post is for anyone who had pytrends in a requirements.txt file and is now deciding what replaces it. The short answer: every unofficial wrapper breaks again the next time Google changes its frontend, so the real choice is who maintains the fix. You can patch it yourself, apply for Google's own alpha, or pay a single-purpose scraper vendor. Or you can call Wire's maintained google_trends actions and skip the patching entirely. Here's what each path costs you, starting with the two that don't involve a vendor at all.


## Path 1: fix the session yourself


The actual bug is narrow enough to patch by hand.[One writeup](https://apiserpent.com/blog/pytrends-dead-google-trends-data-2026) shows the same endpoint pytrends fails on returning a clean 200 once the NID cookie is warmed correctly first, about 15 lines of request code, no library required.[trendspy](https://github.com/sdil87/trendspy) , a newer community library on PyPI (latest release 0.1.6, December 2024), handles that cookie exchange for you and also reaches the newer trending-search surface that pytrends can no longer see.


Both options work today. Neither comes with a warranty. Google doesn't publish this API, it's the same JSON endpoint the Trends website itself calls, and the entire category of unofficial wrapper breaks again the moment Google's frontend team changes a cookie name or a request shape without telling anyone. That's exactly what killed pytrends the first time.


## Path 2: apply for Google's own alpha


Google[announced an official Google Trends API](https://developers.google.com/search/blog/2025/07/trends-api) in alpha in July 2025, open to researchers, journalists, and developers through an application form. It's a real improvement in one specific way: the numbers it returns are **consistently scaled** across requests, which the public Trends website and every unofficial wrapper are not. Ask the same keyword twice on the public UI and the 0-100 index can shift, because it's rescaled against whatever else happened to be in that batch.


It comes with three limits worth knowing before you apply. Access is gated and granted on a rolling basis, so not every applicant gets in, and not immediately. Data lags by roughly 48 hours. And it doesn't cover trending-now search, only the historical interest-over-time and regional surfaces. If your use case needs real-time trending topics, the alpha API can't do it even once you're approved.


## Path 3: pay someone else to maintain the wrapper


This is the most crowded shelf in the whole space, and crowded in a way that's itself a signal. A search for "Google Trends scraper" on Apify alone turns up dozens of competing actors for what is, underneath, the same undocumented endpoint everyone is calling, priced anywhere from[$0.49 per 1,000 results](https://apify.com/blackfalcondata/google-trends-scraper) to[$5 per 1,000 keywords](https://apify.com/signalbench/google-trends-scraper) (plus platform usage on that one since September), depending which one you pick. One of the mid-priced options is literally named["Reliable, Never Charges for Empty Runs"](https://apify.com/0xgollum/reliable-trends-scraper) , and its README opens by quoting the complaint it says other Trends scrapers share in their reviews: "ran for 20 minutes, didn't return anything." That's a vendor responding directly to how often the category burns people. Scrapfly, SerpApi, DataForSEO, and Bright Data all sell the same underlying data as a managed line item too, each with its own pricing and its own SLA, separate from whatever else you're already paying for scraping infrastructure.


Apify's own official actor for this, not a third-party one, has pulled[more than 16,000 users, priced from $0.30 per 1,000 results](https://apify.com/apify/google-trends-scraper) (as of 25 Oct 2026), which says more about how much demand pytrends breaking created than about how good any single option is. Wire sits somewhere else. Its google_trends actions aren't a standalone product with their own price sheet: they're one maintained entry in a catalog of more than 970 sites, billed from the same credits and supported the same way as everything else you call through Anakin.


## Which pytrends methods you need to replace


Strip away the plumbing and nearly every pytrends use case reduces to five data shapes: how interest in a keyword moved over time, how that breaks down by country or city, what else people search alongside it, what's trending right now, and the category taxonomy Trends uses to scope all of the above. pytrends covered these with interest_over_time(), interest_by_region(), related_queries(), trending_searches(), and categories(): the exact five, under different names.


[Wire](https://anakin.io/products/wire) 's catalog carries a maintained google_trends action set that covers the same five, plus two more: a direct multi-keyword comparison and keyword autocomplete with topic-entity IDs attached (useful if you need to disambiguate "jaguar" the car from "jaguar" the animal before you pull a trend line).

None of it needs a cookie you have to warm, a session you have to keep alive across requests, or a GitHub issue to check before you deploy. It's one action in a catalog you're probably already calling for something else: Wire covers more than 970 sites behind the same contract, so this isn't a second vendor relationship. It's seven more rows in a table you already have access to.


## Calling it


With an API key, every Wire action runs through the same two-step async pattern:[submit the task](https://anakin.io/docs/api-reference/wire/execute-task) , then[poll for the result](https://anakin.io/docs/api-reference/wire/get-job) . The key goes in an X-API-Key header.


```text
curl -X POST https://api.anakin.io/v1/wire/task \
-H "X-API-Key: $ANAKIN_API_KEY" \
-H "Content-Type: application/json" \
-d '{
"action_id": "gt_interest_over_time",
"params": {
"keyword": "pytrends",
"timeframe": "today 12-m"
}
}'
```


```text
{
"status": "processing",
"job_id": "7c3f1a2b-4d5e-6f7a-8b9c-0d1e2f3a4b5c",
"poll_url": "/v1/wire/jobs/7c3f1a2b-4d5e-6f7a-8b9c-0d1e2f3a4b5c"
}
```


Poll the poll_url until status flips to completed:


```text
curl https://api.anakin.io/v1/wire/jobs/7c3f1a2b-4d5e-6f7a-8b9c-0d1e2f3a4b5c \
-H "X-API-Key: $ANAKIN_API_KEY"
```

Worldwide interest in the term "pytrends" peaked the first week of June 2026, then fell to zero for five straight weeks from late August into September: people stopped searching for a tool once it stopped being worth searching for. The action that replaces pytrends returned the data that shows pytrends fading, pulled live rather than reconstructed from a cached dashboard. A rerun on 25 Oct 2026 showed the same shape with slightly different numbers, because Trends rescales on every request: the week of Apr 5 read 91 instead of 90, the week of May 31 was still the peak at 100, and seven of the eight weeks from mid-August to early October read zero.


The related-queries action makes the same point from a different angle. A gt_related_queries run for "google trends api" on 25 Oct 2026 returned "official google trends api" as the top related query, and the same phrase was up 350% among rising queries. People who hit the wall are looking for the sanctioned route, which is Path 2 above, with all of its access limits.


If you want to see the data before creating an account, read-only actions like these also run with no key at all. Anakin's[Zero Touch endpoint](https://anakin.io/docs/integrations/ai-agents/zero-touch) , POST /v1/wire-run, takes the same action_id and params and returns the result inline, with no polling. We ran gt_interest_over_time for "pytrends" that way on 25 Oct 2026 and got all 54 weekly points back in one call. The same keyless access works over MCP: an MCP client pointed at Anakin's server with no token gets the wire_read_action tool, so an agent can pull Trends data on its own.

## Where this leaves you


pytrends isn't coming back. Its maintainer said as much when they archived it, and the gap between "archived April 2025" and[more than 900,000 PyPI downloads in the last month](https://pypistats.org/packages/pytrends) (pypistats, 25 Oct 2026) is the gap that keeps producing posts like this one. Patching the cookie flow yourself works until Google changes it again. The official alpha API is the most durable long-term answer if you can get in and don't need trending-now data. Paying a single-purpose scraper vendor works, but you're now tracking uptime and pricing changes on a second tool.


Wire's google_trends catalog is the option built to last: the same data, inside infrastructure you already run other sites through, with no cookie logic for you to maintain when Google changes the underlying flow again, and it will. That becomes Wire's maintenance burden, not yours, which is the difference that counts once you've read the first three paths above.[Browse the full catalog](https://anakin.io/products/wire) or jump straight to the[Wire API reference](https://anakin.io/docs/api-reference/wire) to see every action's exact parameter schema before you wire it in.


This isn't the only Google-adjacent API that stopped being a safe default this year. The[Custom Search JSON API's own shutdown](https://anakin.io/blog/google-custom-search-api-shutdown-what-to-use-instead) followed the same arc: works fine for years, then closes to new usage with limited warning. Worth a read if you're auditing what else in your stack depends on an undocumented or soon-to-sunset Google endpoint.


## FAQ


### What's the easiest replacement for pytrends?


Wire's google_trends catalog, if you don't want to maintain cookie-handling code yourself. It covers the same five core methods pytrends had (interest over time, regional breakdown, related queries, trending searches, the category tree) plus keyword comparison and autocomplete, billed from the same Anakin credit pool as everything else on the platform and maintained the same way as the rest of Wire's catalog of more than 970 sites. Patching pytrends' session bug yourself or applying for Google's alpha API both work too, but neither is maintained for you the way Wire's catalog is.


### Is pytrends completely broken, or does it sometimes still work?


It's inconsistent, not uniformly dead. Some calls succeed depending on the day and your IP's cookie state. The trending-search methods return a hard 404 because Google moved that endpoint. Treat any pytrends call in production as unreliable rather than debugging it as a configuration problem on your end.


### Does the official Google Trends API alpha replace pytrends entirely?


Not yet. It covers interest-over-time and regional data with consistently scaled numbers, but access is application-gated with no guaranteed approval timeline, data lags about 48 hours, and it has no trending-now surface at all.


### Is Google Trends data actual search volume?


No. On the public site, the alpha API, and every unofficial wrapper including Wire's, it's a relative interest index (0-100) scaled against the time range and region you query, not an absolute query count. Nothing in this category, free or paid, publishes true search volume.


### What does trendspy fix that pytrends doesn't?


It handles Google's current cookie-based session requirement correctly and reaches the newer trending-search surface. It's still an unofficial wrapper around the same undocumented endpoint, so it carries the same long-term maintenance risk pytrends did.


### How much does Wire's Google Trends action cost per call?


3 credits for interest-over-time, interest-by-region at 2, related queries and comparison at 3 each, trending searches at 2, suggestions at 3, and the category tree at 1. All billed from the same Anakin credit pool as every other Wire and URL Scraper call, charged only on success.


### Is there a free Google Trends API?


Not an official one you can use today without applying: Google's alpha API is application-gated. pytrends and trendspy are free to install, but both are unofficial wrappers around an undocumented endpoint. Wire's google_trends actions run with no API key through Anakin's Zero Touch endpoint, against a free allowance of 300 credits per IP (as of 26 Oct 2026), so 100 interest-over-time calls at 3 credits each. A free Starter account also comes with 300 one-time credits.
